Read /Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec14/luna/package.md. It holds image section 14 (Soy, rütbe ve en alttakiler) of the frozen surah commentary of surah 103: the Arabic text of the ayat concerned, the Turkish
commentary written on them, the words/roots/branch labels recorded in the frozen surah commentary, and the
whole surah in Arabic. The selected commentary defines your scope; the other inputs supply context.

Find, from the Hebrew Bible, the New Testament, and the Jewish and Christian literature around them (Targum,
Mishnah, Talmud, midrash, pseudepigrapha, Christian apocrypha, Church Fathers, Syriac homilies), every text an
advanced reader of this commentary should have beside it. Judge each text on what it says in its own place, not
on resemblance of a word. Weigh at least:

- paralel: the same figure, scene or story told in the other scripture;
- motif: a shared image, formula, liturgical act or ethical motif without a shared story;
- karsi_anlati: the Qur'an tells it differently, corrects or answers it; the difference is the point;
- soydas: a Hebrew, Aramaic or Syriac cognate of a key word of these ayat and how the other scripture uses it;
- yorum_gelenegi: Jewish or Christian interpretation of a parallel text that changes what the parallel means.

Before grading, work through every distinct scene, object, action, relation, formula and secondary sense
actually developed in the commentary, including any v16 augment additions. Recall direct formulations, repeated
occurrences, nonlexical parallels, relevant reversals and interpretive traditions. Do not let the title, first
scene or already quoted passages stand in for the whole page. For a Buluşmalar section, consider the particular
meetings between images its prose develops. Root/branch labels are not dictionary definitions, evidence of
cognacy or permission to import an undeveloped sense. Do this review internally; output only candidate rows.

Use the package's Semitic root table: for every Arabic root it lists, recall how the corresponding Hebrew or
Aramaic root is used across the Hebrew Bible, passages that play on the same consonants, and passages whose
wording shows a difference from what the ayah says. Propose such passages as soydas (shared root), motif,
paralel or karsi_anlati as fits, and name the basis in `basis` (the root, and whether it is the table's sound
correspondence or your own recollection). Same consonants with an unrelated sense are not a connection.

Every explanation must identify a particular detail or claim in the commentary, the corresponding detail in
the candidate's own context, and what the relationship adds. Shared vocabulary, a broad religious theme or
the same speaker alone is insufficient. Do not invent imagery that neither text supports. A shared word is
not required. Preserve indirect, secondary and contrary readings with a concrete connection; do not choose
one preferred reading. A parallel is not a dependence: say what the texts share, not who borrowed.

Check the speaker, addressee, action, negation and verse boundary in remembered context. Name a neighbouring
verse separately when its own contribution is necessary; proximity alone does not qualify it. Keep Hebrew,
Aramaic, Syriac and Greek quotations short and specific to the cited passage and witness. If exact wording or
numbering is uncertain, explain the connection and uncertainty in English instead of reconstructing a quote.
Label roots, dictionary forms and wording from the source commentary explicitly. Never combine verses into
one quotation. Distinguish WLC's written/ketiv stream from qere and other readings; name another witness when
you rely on it. Discovery is memory-only: the later verifier will open the actual texts and check your claims.

Include every candidate meeting this standard. There is no target list length. Strong means a direct,
specific correspondence, including a secondary feature developed in the prose. Medium means a specific
correspondence with an explicit interpretive bridge. Weak means a plausible, specific connection whose
uncertainty you identify; it still cannot be generic. Counter-narrative is a relationship kind, not weaker
confidence. Model agreement and a follow-up origin never make a claim verified.

Write one TSV row per distinct connection with exactly six tab-separated fields:

strength	tradition	kind	ref	basis	short_explanation

strength: strong, medium, weak. tradition: tevrat (Hebrew Bible and Jewish literature) or incil (New Testament and
Christian literature). kind: paralel, motif, karsi_anlati, soydas, yorum_gelenegi. ref: for the Hebrew Bible and
the New Testament an edition-qualified OSIS reference, one verse per row, no ranges
(WLC:Gen.22.2, WLC:Ps.1.3, SBLGNT:Matt.6.5; consecutive verses on their own rows).
Use Hebrew WLC numbering for Hebrew Bible candidates and SBLGNT numbering for New Testament candidates;
do not silently transfer English/KJV verse numbers. For other works give the work and its place as a reader
cites it (Targum Jonathan on Genesis 22:2;
Genesis Rabbah 56:1; Berakhot 60b; Ephrem, Hymns on Paradise 5:6; Protevangelium of James 8). basis: the words,
scene or motif that carries the link, in a few words. Strongest first. Keep distinct reasons or link kinds for
one passage in separate rows; exact repeated connections are unnecessary. Do not regrade an existing row.
The handoff groups references but preserves each distinct connection for an individual verdict.

## Frozen commentary (Turkish)

İnsanlar kendilerini bir köke bağlar, soylu ya da düşük. Asr kökü bu soyun adıdır: {ar:العنصر والعنصر الأصل والحسب, tr:el-unsur, gloss:unsur, kök ve soydur, source:"ع ص ر,B011"}, {ar:فلان كريم العصير أي كريم النسب, tr:kerîmu'l-asîr, gloss:soyu temiz, source:"ع ص ر,B011"}; aynı kök azatlıların en düşüğünü de adlandırır: {ar:هؤلاء موالينا عصرة أي دنية دون من سواهم, tr:mevâlînâ usratan, gloss:bunlar bizim en alt derecedeki azatlılarımız, source:"ع ص ر,B012"}. Kayıp kelimesinin uzatılmış biçimleri de insanların zayıflarını ve bayağılarını anlatır: {ar:الخناسر الضعاف من الناس, tr:el-hanâsir, gloss:hanâsir, insanların zayıflarıdır, source:"خ س ر,B005"}. Karşısında insan, türün bütünüdür: {ar:الإنس البشر, tr:el-insu'l-beşer, gloss:ins, insan türüdür, source:"ء ن س,B001"}.

Birinci ayetin kelimesi soyu ve rütbeyi çağrıştırırken, ikinci ayet istisnasız "insan" der: kayıp soylu ile düşüğü birlikte kapsar. Ayrımı üçüncü ayet yapar ve onu soya değil, imana ve işe bağlar. Düz anlatım bu eşitlemenin, soy ve rütbe adını taşıyan bir kelimenin hemen ardından geldiğini fark ettirmez. Kur'an soyların kesildiği anı kayıpla birleştirir: {ar:فَإِذَا نُفِخَ فِى ٱلصُّورِ فَلَآ أَنسَابَ بَيْنَهُمْ يَوْمَئِذٍۢ, tr:fe-izâ nufiha fi's-sûri fe-lâ ensâbe beynehum yevmeizin, gloss:sûra üflendiğinde o gün aralarında soy bağı kalmaz, source:23:101}, iki ayet sonra kendini kaybedenler gelir {source:23:103}. Üstünlük ölçüsü de açıkça değiştirilir: {ar:إِنَّ أَكْرَمَكُمْ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ أَتْقَىٰكُمْ, tr:inne ekramekum indallâhi etkâkum, gloss:Allah katında en değerliniz, en çok sakınanınızdır, source:49:13}. Nuh'un kavminin ileri gelenleri ise imanı rütbeyle ölçer: {ar:قَالُوٓا۟ أَنُؤْمِنُ لَكَ وَٱتَّبَعَكَ ٱلْأَرْذَلُونَ, tr:kâlû enu'minu leke vettebeake'l-erzelûn, gloss:sana en aşağılıklar uymuşken biz mi sana inanacağız dediler, source:26:111}; bir başka anlatımda {ar:وَمَا نَرَىٰكَ ٱتَّبَعَكَ إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ هُمْ أَرَاذِلُنَا, tr:ve mâ nerâke'ttebeake illellezîne hum erâzilunâ, gloss:sana ancak aramızdaki en düşüklerin uyduğunu görüyoruz, source:11:27}.

item.text: The brief centers on four links: inherited rank versus moral standing, the inclusion of high and low in “humanity,” elite contempt for low-status followers, and the Hebrew/Aramaic root correspondences where the context supports them. I’m drafting only those candidate rows now.

/bin/bash -lc "cat > enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec14/luna/list.tsv <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.49.3	low/high and rich/poor together	The commentary says al-insan includes noble and low; this psalm explicitly addresses low and high, rich and poor together before warning against confidence in wealth, making its wisdom socially comprehensive.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.62.10	high and low weighed alike	The commentary places noble and lowest ranks inside one loss; this verse says low-born are vanity and high-born a lie, together lighter than breath on the scales, turning rank into shared futility.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.34.19	God shows no partiality to princes or rich	The commentary makes lineage and rank irrelevant to humanity's loss; Job describes the Creator as neither favoring princes nor preferring rich over poor, grounding equal standing in God's making of all.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Lev.19.15	neither poor nor great favored in judgment	The commentary relocates distinction from birth rank to faith and conduct; this law forbids favoring the poor or deferring to the great and requires just judgment, making status irrelevant to assessment.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ezek.18.20	individual guilt, not a father's	The commentary refuses inherited lineage as a criterion; Ezekiel says a son does not bear his father's guilt and each person bears his own, making accountability individual rather than genealogical.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ezek.18.21	repentance and practiced justice	Where the note says the surah distinguishes by faith and deeds, Ezekiel says a wicked person who turns and practices justice and righteousness will live, making changed conduct rather than parentage decisive.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mal.3.18	righteousness and service	The note says the third ayah distinguishes by faith and work; Malachi's promised distinction is between righteous and wicked, and between one who serves God and one who does not, an ethical-religious axis rather than lineage.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5	one Adam; no superior ancestry	The commentary breaks lineage's status claim by including noble and low alike; the Mishnah says Adam was created singly so none can boast that their ancestor is greater, an explicit rabbinic rejection of pedigree ranking.
strong	tevrat	motif	Wisdom of Solomon 6:5	judgment falls severely on rulers	The commentary places high and low within the same human loss; Wisdom warns that judgment falls severely on those in high office, showing that rank increases exposure rather than offering shelter.
strong	tevrat	motif	Wisdom of Solomon 5:8	wealth and boasting fail at judgment	The commentary brings rank and loss together; in the wicked person's postmortem confession, Wisdom asks what wealth and arrogance profited them, exposing status as no protection at judgment.
strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 10:14	rulers overturned, humble raised	The commentary names both high rank and the lowest social position; Sirach says God overturns rulers' thrones and installs the lowly, making earthly rank reversible under divine judgment.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.3.8	fruit worthy of repentance	The commentary says the surah's distinction is made by faith and deeds; John demands conduct that bears fruit worthy of repentance, setting an ethical test beside the following rejection of inherited confidence.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.3.9	Abrahamic descent cannot secure standing	The commentary rejects lineage as the basis of distinction; John warns hearers not to rely on Abraham as father and says God can raise children for Abraham from stones, denying inherited pedigree as a guarantee.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.8.39	Abraham's children must do Abraham's works	The commentary says rank by descent gives way to faith and action; Jesus answers a claim of Abrahamic descent by making Abraham-like deeds the test of true kinship.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.2.6	judgment according to deeds	The commentary assigns distinction to belief and righteous work rather than lineage; Paul says God repays each according to deeds, giving the same non-hereditary measure in a judgment setting.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.2.11	God shows no partiality	The note's human category includes high and low without exception; Paul says God shows no partiality in judgment, removing social or inherited standing as an advantage.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.1.17	impartial judgment of each person's work	The commentary says lineage does not decide who is lost and deeds mark the distinction; Peter describes the Father as judging each person's work impartially, closely joining both claims.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.10.34	God shows no partiality	The commentary includes high and low in the same human category; after Peter's vision opens the message to Gentiles, he says God shows no partiality, removing inherited peoplehood as a barrier.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.10.35	fear of God and right action across nations	The commentary makes faith and deeds the dividing criterion; Peter says a person from any nation who fears God and does what is right is acceptable, explicitly replacing ancestry with religious conduct.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.2.2	rings and clothing mark social rank	The commentary names noble descent and the lowest freedmen; James's assembly scene distinguishes a gold-ringed, finely dressed visitor from a poor person in shabby clothes, making rank's visible signs concrete.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.2.3	preferential seating for the rich	The note says status should not decide human worth; James depicts the rich being offered a good seat while the poor are made to stand or sit below, then condemns the community's class judgment.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.2.5	poor rich in faith and heirs	The commentary says the later ayah distinguishes by faith and work; James says God chose the poor to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, reversing social rank through faith.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.2.9	partiality is sin	The commentary replaces inherited rank with a religious-ethical criterion; James explicitly calls favoritism toward status groups sin, giving the social hierarchy a moral verdict.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.1.26	noble birth among the called	The commentary contrasts lineage and rank with the surah's criterion of faith and deeds; Paul reminds the Corinthians that few were wise, powerful, or well-born when called, showing the community was not selected by elite status.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.1.27	God chooses the weak	The note includes the lowest ranks within humanity; Paul says God chose the world's weak and foolish to shame the strong and wise, reversing the social measure of worth.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.1.28	lowly and despised chosen	The commentary highlights the lowliest freedmen and weak people; Paul says God chose what is low and despised, even what is not, to nullify what is, directly reversing status.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.1.29	no human may boast before God	The commentary removes lineage as a basis for superiority; Paul says God's choice leaves no human able to boast before God, explicitly closing off inherited or social prestige.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Gal.3.28	Jew/Greek and slave/free made one	The commentary says al-insan includes noble and low alike; Paul names Jew/Greek and slave/free distinctions and says they do not divide those in Christ, shifting standing away from inherited and social categories.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.20	rich man's death defeats his security	The commentary pairs rank with human loss; God tells the rich landowner his life is required that night, so accumulated wealth and status cannot secure him from death.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.21	rich toward God	The commentary says the final distinction is not lineage but faith and deeds; Jesus applies the rich fool's story to one who stores treasure for himself but is not rich toward God.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.22	both die; poor man exalted	The commentary includes the high and low in humanity's loss; Luke has both Lazarus and the rich man die, but Lazarus is carried to Abraham's side while the rich man is buried, reversing earthly rank.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.25	life's status reversed after death	The note says rank cannot determine the final distinction; Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in life while Lazarus received bad, but now Lazarus is comforted and he is in anguish.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.20.12	great and small judged by deeds	The commentary says no human rank escapes the encompassing judgment and deeds distinguish; Revelation pictures the dead, great and small, before the throne and says they are judged by what they did.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.1.52	rulers brought down, humble exalted	The commentary sets lineage and high/low rank beside universal human loss; Mary's praise says God brings rulers from thrones and exalts the lowly, a direct reversal of social rank.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.22.2	one Maker of rich and poor	The commentary's al-insan embraces noble and low; Proverbs says rich and poor meet because the Lord made them both, grounding their common humanity in one Creator.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.49.18	wealth does not follow at death	The commentary places status and loss in adjacent ayat; the psalm says a dying rich person carries nothing away and his glory does not descend with him, concretizing why wealth cannot secure the human.
medium	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Eccl.9.2	the same earthly fate for righteous and wicked	The commentary says humanity is in loss while the next ayah marks a believing, righteous exception; Qoheleth says the same fate comes to righteous and wicked, clean and unclean, in the earthly register of death, sharpening the difference in horizon.
medium	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.6.9	Noah righteous amid a corrupt generation	The commentary's Noah scene says elites reject him because low-status people follow; Genesis presents Noah as righteous and blameless amid a corrupt generation, framing the same figure through his conduct without mentioning follower rank.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Sam.16.7	heart over stature and appearance	Samuel initially sees Eliab's stature as kingly, but God says he sees the heart rather than appearance; this parallels the commentary's move away from rank toward an inner moral criterion.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.40.23	princes reduced to nothing	Where the commentary says noble and low ranks share human loss, Isaiah says God reduces princes to nothing and makes rulers as emptiness, portraying status as unable to endure before God.

medium	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Eccl.9.2	the same earthly fate for righteous and wicked	The commentary says humanity is in loss while the next ayah marks a believing, righteous exception; Qoheleth says the same fate comes to righteous and wicked, clean and unclean, in the earthly register of death, sharpening the difference in horizon.
medium	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.6.9	Noah righteous amid a corrupt generation	The commentary's Noah scene says elites reject him because low-status people follow; Genesis presents Noah as righteous and blameless amid a corrupt generation, framing the same figure through his conduct without mentioning follower rank.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Sam.16.7	heart over stature and appearance	Samuel initially sees Eliab's stature as kingly, but God says he sees the heart rather than appearance; this parallels the commentary's move away from rank toward an inner moral criterion.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.40.23	princes reduced to nothing	Where the commentary says noble and low ranks share human loss, Isaiah says God reduces princes to nothing and makes rulers as emptiness, portraying status as unable to endure before God.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Job.14.1	Arabic ء ن س and Hebrew אנוש; table correspondence, BDB notes Arabic cognate	The commentary uses insan for humanity and says no rank escapes loss; Job calls אנוש, the human born of woman, few of days and full of trouble, a direct mortal-human use of the table's Arabic-linked Hebrew root.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.103.16	Arabic ء ن س and Hebrew אנוש; table correspondence, BDB notes Arabic cognate	The commentary glosses insan as the human species and khusr as a shared condition; this verse calls אנוש as fleeting as grass whose days are like grass, using the same human term for vulnerability.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Prov.13.25	Arabic خ س ر and Hebrew חסר; table sound correspondence, unverified	The commentary says the later ayah distinguishes by belief and work; Proverbs contrasts the righteous person's satisfaction with the wicked person's lack, using חסר, the table's unverified sound correspondence, to connect moral standing with shortfall.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.23.2	Arabic خ س ر and Hebrew חסר; table sound correspondence, unverified	The commentary says humanity is in khusr but the next ayah marks an exception; the psalm's speaker says he will not lack under the Lord's shepherding, giving a specific no-lack counterpart and a parallel exception.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Dan.7.13	Arabic ء ن س and Aramaic אנש; table sound correspondence, unverified	The commentary uses insan for the whole human species; Daniel's אנש appears in a singular humanlike figure amid beastly empires, so the cognate's context sharply differs from a collective humanity in loss.
medium	tevrat	motif	Pirkei Avot 4:1	honor earned by honoring others	The commentary contrasts lineage and rank with the later ayah's deeds; Ben Zoma defines the honored person as one who honors others, making honor an ethical practice rather than inherited standing.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.12.50	kinship defined by doing God's will	The commentary brings lineage under a criterion of faith and action; Jesus calls whoever does the Father's will his brother, sister, and mother, replacing natural descent with obedience.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Phil.3.5	ancestral and religious credentials	The commentary calls lineage and rank a human status measure; Paul lists circumcision, Israelite identity, and Benjaminite descent among his credentials, supplying a concrete pedigree catalogue.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Phil.3.7	former gains counted as loss	The commentary places lineage/status next to khusr; after listing his pedigree and religious standing, Paul counts those former gains as loss because of Christ, a striking revaluation of inherited prestige.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Mark.2.16	elite objection to eating with sinners	The commentary's Noah accusers discredit him because low-status people follow; scribes object when Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners, showing religious elites policing association with social outsiders.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.7.49	elite contempt for the crowd	The commentary's Noah narrative has elites call his followers the lowest; Pharisees dismiss the crowd as ignorant of the law and accursed, a close instance of status-bearing leaders discrediting ordinary people.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.4.13	ordinary followers recognized with Jesus	The commentary says Noah's elite opponents treat low status as grounds to reject his message; authorities see Peter and John as uneducated and ordinary yet recognize their association with Jesus, a counterexample to status-based dismissal.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.15.22	all die in Adam, life in Christ	The commentary says khusr encompasses humanity without regard to rank; Paul says all die in Adam and all are made alive in Christ, placing humanity under shared death and framing life through Christ.
